loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 4, "The four authentication modes you choose at install" table, Direct Access row
orig: When using Direct Access, there is no RBAC set on Veeam Kasten, and any user who has access to the dashboard can perform all Veeam Kasten operations, which is not advisable if granular access is needed [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.220].
prop: When using Direct Access, there is no authentication configured and no RBAC set on Veeam Kasten, so any user who has access to the dashboard can perform all Veeam Kasten operations — including deleting a restore point — with no authenticated identity to record against the action. Treat Direct Access as lab-only; it should never be the exposure choice on a cluster protecting anything you would have to account for [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.220].
why: The table already establishes that Direct Access has 'No authentication configuration' and 'no RBAC set,' but frames the consequence as merely 'not advisable if granular access is needed.' For a production-accountability audience that understates the finding: with no authentication, there is no identity to log against any action at all, which is a disqualifying fact for anything beyond a lab, not a granularity preference. This sharpens language the module already supports rather than adding a new claim.

orig: What you should see: Helm confirms the repository was added. This is the only step in the module that talks to the internet rather than to your cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4].
prop: Correct or qualify this claim, and add it as a "before you start" prerequisite: confirm the cluster nodes have image-pull reachability (public registry, or an internal mirror/air-gapped registry per your environment) before running the Helm install in Section 3, since that install pulls a container image for every Veeam Kasten service Pod. Note that this module's own air-gapped pre-flight command two sections later (`bash /dev/stdin -i repo.example.com/k10tools:9.0.2`) already shows a registry substitution, which is the tell that image-pull reachability is a real, separate dependency from the Helm chart-repo add shown here.
why: As written, an implementer in a network-restricted environment has no reason to check registry/image-pull access before the install window, because the module explicitly (and incorrectly, by its own later evidence) tells them only one step needs the internet. If node egress to the image registry is blocked, every Kasten Pod sits in ImagePullBackOff with nothing earlier in the runbook having flagged the risk — that is a mid-install stall with no prior warning, which is exactly what this lens exists to catch.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 6 of 6 — "Pointing it at a Veeam repository"
orig: Provide the DNS name or the IP address of the Veeam backup server in the Veeam Backup Server field; the Veeam Backup Server API Port field is pre-configured with the installation default value and may be changed if necessary; specify the name of a backup repository on this server in the Backup Repository field [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.336].
prop: [VERIFY: does the wizard also ask for a Veeam Backup & Replication user account, API credential, or token to authenticate this location profile to the backup server — and if so, what permissions does that account need on the B&R server?] Add whatever the source page states about authentication to this field list; if the profile genuinely authenticates with no credential (e.g., trust is established some other way), say so explicitly rather than leaving the field silent.
why: As a VDP admin this is the one step in the whole course that connects Veeam Kasten back to infrastructure I already own and secure, and the field list — DNS/IP, API port, repository name — has no authentication step at all. I cannot tell whether I need to create a B&R API user first, whether the connection is unauthenticated, or whether I'm missing a field the dashboard actually shows. I would stall here rather than guess at credentials for a production backup server.

orig: If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315] — this is the setting that protects exported restore points from tampering: in a locked bucket, restore point data cannot be deleted or modified within the set protection period, even with administrator privileges, so a clean copy survives an attacker who has obtained privileged object store credentials [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.341].
prop: If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315] — this is the setting that protects exported restore points from tampering: in a locked bucket, restore point data cannot be deleted or modified within the set protection period, even with administrator privileges, so a clean copy survives an attacker who has obtained privileged object store credentials [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.341]. Treat this toggle as the default for every production export location profile, not only the one behind Kasten Disaster Recovery — a profile without it is the first thing a CISO will flag.
why: Module 04 gives immutability the strong, explicit 'the guide states this strongly' treatment for Kasten Disaster Recovery profiles. The same control, for ordinary application export profiles, is buried as a single conditional bullet inside a dense paragraph in Module 03 with no equivalent emphasis — a governance-critical setting is present in the content but not surfaced with the weight a director would expect given how hard the course leans on it elsewhere.

orig: Depending on your underlying infrastructure, you might also need to provide access credentials as specified elsewhere for public cloud providers [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.99].
prop: Name or point to where "elsewhere" actually is for each platform this audience is likely to run — Azure, GCP, and on-premises vSphere/Tanzu — the way the module already does for AWS immediately below this sentence. If the referenced material lives in the Infrastructure Profile section (Section 5) rather than at install time, say that explicitly.
why: The module gives a full, copy-pasteable install command for AWS and nothing runnable for any other platform. A VDP admin whose Kubernetes cluster runs on Azure, GCP, or on-prem vSphere has no path forward inside the module and has to go looking for credential flags on their own before the install command will even attempt to run.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 4 of 6 — "The four authentication modes you choose at install"
orig: Basic Authentication requires you to generate htpasswd credentials by either using an online tool or via the htpasswd binary found on most systems, and then supply the resulting string with the helm install or upgrade command [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.221].
prop: [VERIFY: does Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.221 give the exact htpasswd invocation (binary, flags, hash algorithm) the product expects?] If so, quote it as a code block the way every other command in this module is quoted verbatim.
why: Every other command in Module 03 is given as an exact, copy-pasteable line with a citation. This is the one place I'm told to "use a tool" with no invocation shown — I'd have to leave the module to find the right htpasswd flags, and getting the hash format wrong here means a broken login rather than an obvious error.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 2 of 6 — "What a good result looks like"
orig: Where a provisioner has no deletion policy set, the same output reports it plainly as Missing deletionPolicy, using default [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.872].
prop: State plainly whether this line is a pass condition I can proceed past, or a stop-and-fix condition — i.e., is the default deletion policy acceptable to install against, or should I set one explicitly on the VolumeSnapshotClass before continuing to Section 3?
why: This is presented as an example output line with no verdict. Reading pre-flight output for the first time, I have no way to tell from the module alone whether "using default" means I'm clear to install or that I have a follow-up action before I do — exactly the kind of ambiguous result the readiness checklist above it is supposed to resolve for me.

orig: In the unlikely scenario that pods are stuck in any other state, the documentation directs you to the support documentation to debug further [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.101].
prop: Add a "before you escalate" note on the safe retry path: is it safe to `helm uninstall k10 --namespace kasten-io` and re-run the install, or does the namespace / catalog PVC need to be cleaned up first? If the source doesn't say, flag it as a question for the author rather than leaving it silent.
why: This is the only contingency instruction in the entire install runbook, and it is "go to support docs." As a first-time implementer mid-install with pods not reaching Running, I don't know whether to wait, retry from scratch, or whether retrying could leave the namespace or PVCs in a worse state. No retry/rollback guidance is the exact execution blind spot my review lens exists to flag.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Hero, "Assumed before you start" list — "A shell" item
orig: A shell — this module is command-line first. The dashboard comes after the install, not before it.
prop: A shell — this module is command-line first, the way your first Veeam Backup & Replication install was a setup wizard before there was a console to click through: Veeam Kasten's own dashboard is a product it deploys, so there is no GUI path to reach before the platform exists. The dashboard comes after the install, not before it.
why: The flat "command-line first" framing is honest, but it lands a little cold for a GUI-preferring reader without saying why no GUI path exists. Module 02 already built the groundwork for this reassurance with its installer-package-plus-answer-file analogy for Helm; Module 03 just doesn't call back to it at the exact moment a GUI-preferring admin would want the reassurance. The proposed addition adds no new product claim, only a callback to an analogy the course already established.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section "The Helm install", "Where the Veeam Data Platform parallel stops" field-tip
orig: the documentation recommends including Veeam Kasten deployment and configuration as part of a GitOps solution
prop: the documentation recommends including Veeam Kasten deployment and configuration as part of a GitOps solution — GitOps here just means treating the install command and its flags as version-controlled files that redeploy the same way every time, the way you might already keep a build script for standing up a new backup server
why: "GitOps" appears twice in this course (here and in Module 03's storage-integration section) and is never named or defined outright. The surrounding sentence in each case does enough work that a reader can infer the practical meaning, but the term itself is exactly the kind of Kubernetes-ecosystem word a backup admin would nod through in a meeting without admitting they don't know it. A short inline gloss, grounded in the course's own next sentence ("keep the install command and its flags in version control"), closes this without inventing anything.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section "Your first location profile" — Kopia paragraph
orig: Veeam Kasten creates Kopia repositories in object store locations, using Kopia as a data mover, which implicitly provides support to deduplicate, encrypt and compress data at rest — the three things that keep your object storage bill down and your exported data unreadable at rest, with nothing for you to configure or remember
prop: Veeam Kasten creates Kopia repositories in object store locations, using Kopia as a data mover, which implicitly provides support to deduplicate, encrypt and compress data at rest — much the same as a VBK file already gives you today, just done here by Kopia instead of Veeam Backup & Replication — the three things that keep your object storage bill down and your exported data unreadable at rest, with nothing for you to configure or remember
why: This paragraph explains what Kopia does clearly enough, but reads like a new capability being introduced rather than a familiar one. It's a missing-parallel moment: dedup, encryption, and compression at rest is exactly what a VBK already does, and saying so explicitly would reassure rather than add a new thing to track. The parallel is grounded entirely in backup-side facts I already know; it makes no new claim about Kasten.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 4, "Two details are worth carrying forward" paragraph
orig: token-based authentication is always enabled as a secondary authentication type to let Veeam Kasten Multi-Cluster Manager components and Veeam Backup & Replication services work with Veeam Kasten [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.220].
prop: token-based authentication is always enabled as a secondary authentication type to let Veeam Kasten Multi-Cluster Manager components and Veeam Backup & Replication services work with Veeam Kasten [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.220]. Veeam Kasten Multi-Cluster Manager is named here only as an authentication detail — it is the fleet-wide console where a director would look for a compliance rollup across every cluster, not the single-cluster dashboard this course covers, and it deserves a pointer of its own rather than a footnote.
why: This course, by design, covers a single cluster, so a full treatment of Multi-Cluster Manager is out of scope. But it is the natural answer to 'how do I prove program health across my whole fleet to my VP,' and currently a learner would have to already know the product exists to recognize this passing mention as a signpost to it.

orig: To create a location profile, click Create New Profile on the profiles page [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
prop: Add a "before you start" prerequisite noting that cluster nodes need outbound network reachability to the chosen destination — the object storage endpoint, or the Veeam backup server's DNS/IP and API port — before profile validation will succeed.
why: In Veeam Data Platform, checking repository or Cloud Connect reachability is a standing pre-implementation habit. This module never states it as a prerequisite, so a firewalled path would only surface as an unexplained validation failure on the profile card, with nothing earlier telling me to check it first.

prop: Add a one-line note that `--watch` streams continuously and does not exit on its own — press Ctrl+C once every pod shows Running.
why: Small friction for someone who has never used `kubectl --watch` before: the command never returns control, and nothing says so. Easy to fix, and it's the kind of thing that makes a first-timer think something is stuck.

orig: This walkthrough is abbreviated. The Create Infrastructure Profile wizard has three steps — Name and Provider, Configuration, and Summary — and the two screens below are the two the documentation illustrates [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. Treat them as a shape to recognise rather than a complete click path.
prop: For the vSphere case specifically — the most likely on-prem storage integration for this course's audience, since they already run vSphere — point to exactly where the complete click path and required vCenter permissions are documented.
why: The module is honest about the gap, which I appreciate, but the audience most likely to need this exact profile (a VDP admin already running vSphere CNS) is left with a shape to recognize rather than a path to execute, for the one integration that would otherwise be their most familiar step in the whole course.

prop: Distinguish reading/study time from hands-on execution time, or add a rough execution-time range separate from the module's own read-through estimate (e.g., typical elapsed time to run the full runbook against a healthy cluster with CSI snapshot support already validated).
why: "~40 minutes" reads as the time to read the module and take the quiz, not the time to actually run pre-flight, install, dashboard exposure, storage annotation, and a location profile against a live cluster. Planning a change window off this number would badly under-book the work.
